question: A friend sees an empty café and says it must be closing down. You reply, “Let’s not jump to conclusions.” What are you suggesting?
choices: Wait for more information before deciding.
Keep your opinion to yourself in public.
Ask the owner to make a decision soon.
Agree on one explanation before leaving.
note: To “jump to conclusions” is to decide before you have enough evidence. The café could simply be between its busy periods.

question: “We can rule out a flat battery. The camera works with the same battery in it.” What has the speaker done?
choices: Removed one possible explanation.
Found the exact cause of the problem.
Decided to replace the battery anyway.
Put the investigation off until later.
note: Ruling something out removes it from the possibilities. It doesn’t automatically tell you which remaining explanation is right.

picture.alt: A camera beside a blank photograph.

question: “He says he took the last ferry at midnight, but the last one left at eleven. His story doesn’t add up.” What is the problem?
choices: The details don’t make sense together.
The story takes too long to tell.
The speaker has forgotten the ticket price.
The ending is too easy to predict.
note: Here “add up” means make sense. A detail that doesn’t fit needs checking; the person may have mixed up a time rather than invented the whole story.

picture.alt: A ferry beside an İstanbul skyline.

question: Looking at a blurry photo, Ada says, “As far as I can tell, nobody is inside the boat.” How certain is she?
choices: That is her judgement from what she can see.
She has checked the boat in person.
She thinks the photo gives no information at all.
Someone on the boat has confirmed it.
note: “As far as I can tell” leaves room for a mistake or a detail you can’t see. “I’ve checked” would claim stronger evidence.

question: “In hindsight, we should have checked the weather before leaving.” When does the speaker see the better choice?
choices: Now, after seeing how the trip turned out.
Before the trip, while choosing a route.
Only if someone else agrees about the weather.
Next time, when the forecast becomes available.
note: “In hindsight” introduces a judgement made with knowledge you gained afterwards. It’s useful when reflecting on what you could do differently next time.

picture.alt: A travel suitcase with a blank tag.

question: Your partner says a photo shows a protest because a crowd is carrying signs. You can’t read the signs, and some people are wearing running numbers. What do you say?
choices: It could be, though the numbers suggest it might be a race. Can we enlarge it?
That’s an interesting thought. What do you think they’re protesting about?
Shall we describe the buildings first and come back to the people later?
You’ve spotted the signs. Let’s use your explanation for our presentation.
note: “It could be, though…” acknowledges the idea and tests it against another detail. Asking what they’re protesting about already assumes it is a protest. What detail would settle the question?

picture.alt: A camera beside a blank photograph.

question: The cake has disappeared from the shared kitchen. Someone says, “It must have been Leo. He was in there.” You also saw two other people enter. What do you say?
choices: He was there, but so were other people. Has anyone asked if the cake was moved?
Let’s ask Leo to replace it, and we can all share the new one.
Could we speak to Leo privately so he doesn’t feel embarrassed?
Shall we bring another cake tomorrow and leave this for now?
note: Being in the kitchen doesn’t establish who took the cake or whether anyone ate it. A private conversation is considerate, but treating Leo as responsible still goes beyond the evidence.

picture.alt: A cooking pot and wooden spoon.

question: Two classmates disagree about when a photo was taken. One points to long shadows; the other remembers setting the camera’s clock incorrectly. You need a reliable date for a display. What do you suggest?
choices: Could we check the event programme? Neither of those gives us a reliable date.
The shadows are a useful clue. Shall we label it as an evening photograph?
Could we use the camera’s date and add that it may be inaccurate?
Would you both be comfortable choosing a date somewhere between your guesses?
note: The programme offers another source to check. A note about an uncertain camera date is honest, but you still have a way to look for a reliable one. Shadows may suggest a time of day, not a calendar date.

picture.alt: A clock beside a blank calendar.

question: A café owner thinks a new menu caused last week’s rise in customers. A street festival happened outside that week too. She asks what you make of the figures. What do you say?
choices: The menu may have helped, but the festival could explain the rise too.
It sounds promising. Shall we celebrate the success of the new menu?
The festival sounds fun. Did you get a chance to go outside?
Could we ask the chef which of the new dishes they enjoyed making most?
note: Both changes could have affected the figures. Celebrating the menu’s success would be reasonable once you had better evidence of its effect. What could the owner compare next week?

question: You said a shop had closed permanently. Your partner shows you a notice saying it will reopen after repairs. You’re about to record your joint report. What do you say?
choices: You’re right. I missed that notice. I’ll change my part before we record.
Thanks for finding that. Shall we include both our opinions in the report?
That’s useful. Could you mention it after I’ve finished my original version?
Good spot. Shall we keep the report as it is and explain if anyone asks?
note: The notice gives you a reason to revise the claim before recording. Presenting both views suits an unresolved question; here one view has been corrected by direct information.

picture.alt: A sealed envelope with a postage stamp.

question: Your group is describing a lost bag. You’re sure it was blue, but you only caught a glimpse of the label. Someone asks whether the label said “Mina”. What do you say?
choices: I’m sure about the colour, but I didn’t get a clear enough look at the name.
Mina sounds familiar. Shall we put that down so we have something to go on?
Could we finish describing the straps before we talk about the label?
I’d rather let someone else describe the whole bag in case I get anything wrong.
note: You can separate what you remember clearly from what you don’t. Letting someone else take over would avoid a guess, but it would also withhold the colour you do know.

picture.alt: A travel suitcase with a blank tag.

question: A friend shares a cropped screenshot saying tomorrow’s train is cancelled. It shows no date or route, and you both have tickets. She’s about to book an expensive taxi. What do you say?
choices: Before we book, could we check our train on the operator’s website?
That’s thoughtful of you. Shall we split the cost of the taxi equally?
Could you send the screenshot to the others so they can change their plans too?
Shall we wait until we reach the station tomorrow and ask someone there?
note: The missing date and route make the screenshot uncertain evidence for your journey. Asking at the station could help, but checking now gives you time to plan without paying for an unnecessary taxi.

question: Your group missed a museum visit after using last year’s opening hours. You’re planning another visit and have found a current page with a different closing time. What do you say?
choices: Let’s use this year’s hours and check for any changes the day before we go.
Could we arrive an hour earlier than we did last time, just to be safe?
Shall we ask everyone to be more punctual for this visit?
Would it help to book a café nearby in case we miss the museum again?
note: The problem was the information you used. Arriving earlier might help, but checking the current hours tackles that cause. A backup café is useful after you’ve made the main plan reliable.

picture.alt: The columned front of the Pantheon.

question: A photo shows a bicycle lying beside a tree. Your partner says the rider must have hit it. You can’t see damage or a rider, and the task asks you to distinguish observation from possibility. What do you say?
choices: We can see the bike on its side. A collision is one possible explanation.
That would make an interesting story. Shall we describe the rider’s journey?
Could we call it a minor collision so we don’t make it sound too serious?
Shall we leave the bike out of our description since we don’t know what happened?
note: You can describe the bike’s position without claiming to know how it got there. “A minor collision” still claims a collision happened. What other explanation could fit the same photo?

picture.alt: A bicycle and a pink cycling jersey.

question: Two witnesses say the hall’s lights went out before the music stopped. You think a power cut explains both, but nobody has checked with the building manager. Your group needs a sentence to end its report. What do you say?
choices: A power cut seems likely, though we still need the manager to confirm it.
We’ve heard enough to say that a power cut definitely caused the interruption.
We should avoid mentioning a possible cause until the manager has replied.
The witnesses were helpful, so let’s end by thanking them for their time.
note: “Seems likely” matches the evidence while leaving the conclusion open. Waiting for confirmation would suit a report that required a fully verified cause. Here you can give a provisional conclusion and say what remains to be checked.
